claims.text: An ML interatomic potential trained on configurations around fusion and high-temperature phase boundaries can accurately reproduce solid- and liquid-phase free energies in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
The proposed ML workflow will cost substantially less than explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics and TOR-TILD workflows.
Descriptors can be made sensitive to vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration interactions.
Active learning can identify the most informative configurations near fusion interfaces and phase boundaries.
The method is proposed for temperatures from approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the melting temperature.
The proposed scope extends from elemental and binary systems to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Accurate representation of structural fluctuations, anharmonic effects, and electron–vibration coupling determines the ML model's fidelity across the phase transition.
Selecting informative phase-transition configurations through active learning allows the ML potential to approximate the full ab initio free-energy surface efficiently.
Tailored descriptors preserve vibrational-entropy, anharmonic, and electron–vibration-coupling effects.
Preserving these physical effects will keep phase free energies, melting temperatures, and related thermodynamic observables accurate.
The ML workflow will achieve approximately 5–10% error relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
The ML workflow will reduce computational cost by approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The ML workflow will scale better than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
The expected validity domain comprises systems near fusion whose thermodynamics are dominated by vibrational and anharmonic effects.
Uncertainty increases with extreme compositional complexity or dominant electron–vibration interactions outside the descriptor's training domain.
Deviation greater than approximately 10% in phase free-energy differences, melting temperature, or latent heat relative to a benchmark would falsify the accuracy prediction.
A computational-efficiency improvement of less than one order of magnitude would falsify the cost-reduction prediction.
